blocks.text: Transport, communication and trade: why they matter

Resources are not found where people need them. Coal may be mined in one region, steel made in a second, and cars sold in a third. **Transport** moves people and goods, **communication** moves information, and **trade** is the exchange of goods and services. Together they form the network that joins producers and consumers across the world. The quality of this network depends on the physical environment, the level of technology, the wealth of the country and the policy of its government. Transport is judged on four things: cost, speed, safety and carrying capacity, and no single mode is best on all four.
The voluntary exchange of goods and services between people or countries. Trade between countries is international trade; its value is recorded as exports and imports.
Land transport: roads and railways

**Roads** are the most widely used land transport for short distances and offer flexibility and door-to-door service. Road density is higher in developed countries, and many road systems are paved and metalled. Some roads are important continental links. The **Trans-Canada Highway** crosses Canada from coast to coast. The **Alaska Highway** links Dawson Creek in Canada with Fairbanks in Alaska. The **Pan-American Highway** links the countries of North, Central and South America, and the **Stuart Highway** runs from Darwin to Port Augusta in Australia.

**Railways** are best for carrying heavy goods and many passengers over long distances. The **rail network** is densest in Europe, the north-eastern part of North America and parts of Asia, because of the high level of industry and population there. Railway systems need heavy investment in tracks and so they are found where traffic is large. **Trans-continental railways** run from one end of a continent to the other. The **Trans-Siberian Railway** runs across Russia from St Petersburg in the west to Vladivostok on the Pacific coast, and it is the longest double-tracked, electrified trans-continental line. In North America the Canadian Pacific and Union Pacific lines link the east and west coasts, and the Trans-Australian Railway joins Sydney and Perth. The Orient Express ran between Paris and Istanbul.

blocks.problem: A country has an area of 2,000,000 sq km and a total railway length of 100,000 km. Find its railway density per 100 sq km, and say what it would be if the area were halved with the same track.
blocks.solution: Railway density = length of line / area. For 100 sq km, density = (100,000 / 2,000,000) x 100 = 5 km per 100 sq km. If the area is halved to 1,000,000 sq km with the same track, density = (100,000 / 1,000,000) x 100 = 10 km per 100 sq km, which is double the earlier value. A higher density shows a more closely spaced network.
blocks.answer: 5 km per 100 sq km; it would become 10 km per 100 sq km

blocks.text: Water transport: inland waterways and ocean routes

Water transport is the cheapest for heavy, bulky goods, and it needs little fuel per tonne. **Inland waterways** use rivers, canals and lakes. The Rhine, the Danube, the Great Lakes with the St Lawrence Seaway, and the Mississippi system are leading examples. The Rhine in Europe carries a heavy traffic between the North Sea and Switzerland; Rotterdam lies at its mouth. Depth, width and freedom from ice and rapids make a river navigable.

**Ocean routes** are free highways with no cost for track building, and they carry most of the world's long-distance trade by volume. The **North Atlantic sea route** between eastern North America and north-western Europe is the busiest, because it links two of the most industrialised and richest regions. The **Mediterranean-Indian Ocean route**, passing through the **Suez Canal** (opened 1869, about 160 km long as per NCERT), joins the Mediterranean with the Red Sea and shortens the route between Europe and southern and eastern Asia by avoiding the voyage around Africa. The **Cape of Good Hope route** is used by ships that cannot use the Suez Canal. The **Panama Canal** (opened 1914, about 72 km as per NCERT) connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and shortens the route between the east and west coasts of the Americas. Other routes include the North Pacific, South Pacific and South Atlantic routes.

blocks.problem: A ship travelling between two ports can go round the Cape of Good Hope (21,000 km) or through the Suez Canal (12,000 km). If it sails at 20 km per hour, how many days does the canal route save? (Distances are given for this problem only.)
blocks.solution: Distance saved = 21,000 - 12,000 = 9,000 km. Time saved = distance saved / speed = 9,000 / 20 = 450 hours. In days, 450 / 24 = 18.75 days. So the canal route saves nearly 19 days, which also saves fuel and the wages of the crew.

blocks.text: Air transport and intercontinental routes

Air transport is the fastest, and the most costly, mode. It is especially suited for perishable goods, mail, high-value cargo and long-distance passengers, and for places that cannot be reached by land. It is also the most affected by weather and needs airports and costly aircraft. The densest **intercontinental air routes** are those that join the great industrial and commercial regions: the North Atlantic route between North America and Europe is the busiest, followed by the routes between Europe and Asia, and across the Pacific between North America and East Asia. Large hub airports in cities such as London, New York and Singapore serve as transfer points.
Oil and gas pipelines

**Pipelines** carry liquids and gases such as crude oil, natural gas and water, and also solids in the form of slurry (for example coal mixed with water). They are most useful for moving oil and gas from fields to refineries and ports and then to consumers, without a break in the journey. They need a heavy investment, but running costs are low and losses are small. In the United States, long pipelines link the Gulf coast oil and gas fields to the cities of the north-east. In Russia, pipelines carry oil and gas from the fields of Siberia to Europe. A fixed route and the risk of leaks are the drawbacks.
Satellite communication and cyberspace

**Satellite communication** uses satellites in orbit, often geostationary ones, to relay telephone, television, internet and weather data. It needs no cable, and so it serves ships, aircraft and remote areas. **Cyberspace** is the world of electronic networks created by the internet, a space in which people can communicate, shop (e-commerce), study (e-learning) and work (e-governance) without moving. It has made distance less important, but it has also created a gap, called the digital divide, between those who have access and those who do not.
International trade: basis, patterns, ports and the WTO

Trade between countries rests on three main bases: **differences in national resources** such as minerals, climate and soil; **differences in the stage of economic development and in skills**; and the **extent of foreign investment and the transport facilities** available. A country that can make a good at a lower opportunity cost than another has a comparative advantage in it, so both gain from specialisation and exchange. Trade may be bilateral, between two countries, or multilateral, between many. Over time the pattern has changed. The share of manufactured goods has risen, services and information trade have grown, and the volume of trade among developing countries has increased.

**Ports are gateways of international trade**, since goods enter or leave a country through them. A port is where land and water transport meet, and it needs a deep and sheltered harbour and a good hinterland. Types include **oil ports**, **comprehensive ports** which handle varied cargo, **entrepôt ports** that collect goods for re-export (Singapore is a classic example), and **naval ports**. Rotterdam, at the mouth of the Rhine, serves as the gateway to Europe.

The international organisation that came into being on 1 January 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, 1948), with its headquarters in Geneva; it sets the rules of trade between nations and settles disputes.

The **role of the WTO** is to administer trade agreements, to act as a forum for trade negotiations, to settle disputes between members, and to promote free and fair trade by reducing tariffs and other barriers. Supporters say it widens markets and cuts prices. Critics, mostly from developing countries, argue that the rules favour rich countries, and that free trade can harm local producers, workers and the environment.

Revision: Trans-Siberian (St Petersburg to Vladivostok) is the longest trans-continental railway. The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red Sea; the Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific. The North Atlantic route is the busiest sea and air route. WTO was formed in 1995, replaced GATT, and is based in Geneva. Trade depends on differences in resources and development, not on similarity.

Common mistakes: (1) Swapping the Suez and Panama canals. (2) Placing the Trans-Siberian Railway in Canada. (3) Assuming that countries with similar resources trade the most. (4) Saying that WTO fixes prices or exchange rates; it deals with trade rules. (5) Forgetting that figures such as canal lengths are as per NCERT and that question stems give any other data needed.

questions.stem: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs across which country from St Petersburg to Vladivostok?
questions.explanation: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the famous trans-continental line of Russia, running from St Petersburg in the west to Vladivostok on the Pacific coast in the east. Canada and Australia have their own trans-continental lines, and it is not located in China.

optionRationale.1: Canada has the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National lines.
optionRationale.3: Australia has the Trans-Australian line from Sydney to Perth.
optionRationale.4: The line is not in China; its route lies wholly in Russia.

questions.stem: In world transport geography, the Suez Canal joins
options: the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea
the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea
the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, joins the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea, which shortens the route between Europe and southern and eastern Asia. The Panama Canal joins the Atlantic and Pacific.

optionRationale.2: The Red Sea is joined to the Mediterranean and not to the Arabian Sea by the canal itself.
optionRationale.4: The Black Sea and Caspian Sea are not joined by the Suez Canal.

questions.objective: Recall the location of the Suez Canal

questions.stem: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) replaced which earlier arrangement in 1995?
questions.explanation: The WTO came into existence on 1 January 1995 and replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, GATT, which had operated since 1948. OPEC, the IMF and NAFTA are different bodies or agreements.

optionRationale.2: OPEC is an organisation of oil-producing countries.
optionRationale.3: The IMF deals with international monetary matters.
optionRationale.4: NAFTA was a regional trade agreement of North America.

questions.objective: Identify GATT as the predecessor of WTO

questions.stem: In the study of communication, the term cyberspace refers to
options: the world of networks formed by computers and the internet
questions.explanation: Cyberspace is the virtual world of electronic networks, created by interlinked computers and the internet, where people communicate, trade and learn without being physically present. It has no physical territory.

optionRationale.1: It has nothing to do with atmospheric layers.
optionRationale.3: A satellite orbit is a physical path, not cyberspace.

questions.stem: Match the transport link in List-I with its description in List-II.
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea (II). The Panama Canal joins the Atlantic and Pacific (I). The Trans-Siberian is Russia's east-west railway (III), and the Pan-American Highway links the countries of the Americas (IV).

optionRationale.2: This gives the Suez Canal the Russian railway description.
optionRationale.4: This gives Panama the Russian railway and Trans-Siberian the ocean link.

questions.objective: Match transport links with their descriptions

right: I. Joins the Atlantic and Pacific oceans
II. Joins the Mediterranean and Red Sea
IV. Road linking North, Central and South America

questions.stem: A country exports goods worth 480 units and imports goods worth 420 units. Its trade surplus as a percentage of its exports is
questions.explanation: Trade surplus = 480 - 420 = 60 units. As a percentage of exports, 60/480 x 100 = 12.5 per cent. The figure 14.3 per cent is the surplus as a share of imports (60/420), which is not what is asked.

optionRationale.1: 10 per cent does not follow from 60/480.
optionRationale.3: 14.3 per cent uses imports, not exports, as the base.
optionRationale.4: 87.5 per cent is imports as a share of exports (420/480).

questions.objective: Compute trade surplus as a share of exports

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Countries trade with one another.
Reason (R): Countries differ in resources, skills and levels of development, so each can gain by specialising in what it can produce best.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Differences in resources, climate, skills and stage of development mean no country can make everything cheaply. Specialisation and exchange raise total welfare, so the reason correctly explains why trade occurs.

optionRationale.2: The reason explains the assertion directly, so option 2 is wrong.
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true, so option 3 is wrong.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true, so it cannot be false.

questions.stem:
Consider the statements.
A. The Suez Canal shortens the sea route between Europe and southern Asia.
B. The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
C. The Trans-Siberian Railway lies mainly in Canada.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is correct since the Suez Canal avoids the voyage around Africa. B is correct since the Panama Canal joins the two oceans. C is wrong because the Trans-Siberian Railway lies in Russia.

optionRationale.1: C is false, so this pair cannot be right.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so this pair cannot be right.
optionRationale.3: C is false, so it cannot be the only correct statement.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on canals and railways

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a function of the WTO?
options: Printing the currency of member countries
Fixing the price of crude oil
Settling trade disputes among its members
questions.explanation: The WTO administers trade agreements, provides a forum for negotiations and settles disputes between members. It does not print currency, fix oil prices or construct ports, because those tasks belong to other institutions.

optionRationale.1: Currency printing belongs to central banks.
optionRationale.2: Oil prices are not fixed by the WTO.
optionRationale.4: Port construction is done by governments and port authorities.

questions.objective: Describe the role of the WTO

questions.stem: A country has 2,000,000 sq km of area and 100,000 km of railway line. Its railway density per 100 sq km is
questions.explanation: Railway density per 100 sq km = (100,000 / 2,000,000) x 100 = 5 km. The ratio 100,000/2,000,000 is 0.05 km per sq km, and multiplying by 100 gives 5. The other values come from errors in the powers of ten.

optionRationale.2: 2 km is not obtained from the data.
optionRationale.3: 20 km is four times too high.
optionRationale.4: 0.5 km is ten times too low.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The Suez Canal shortens the sea route between Europe and southern and eastern Asia.
Reason (R): The Suez Canal was opened in 1869.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The assertion is true: ships avoid the long voyage around Africa. The reason (the year of opening) is also true but it does not explain the shortening, which is explained by the canal joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

optionRationale.1: The reason does not explain the shortening of the route.
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true, so it cannot be false.
optionRationale.4: The reason is true, so option 4 is wrong.

questions.objective: Separate a true fact from the explanation

questions.stem: A ship can go round the Cape of Good Hope (21,000 km) or through the Suez Canal (12,000 km), sailing at 20 km per hour. How many days does the canal route save?
questions.explanation: The distance saved is 21,000 - 12,000 = 9,000 km. At 20 km per hour this takes 9,000/20 = 450 hours. Dividing by 24 gives 18.75 days. The value 9.0 days wrongly treats the 9,000 km saved as if it were a time.

optionRationale.1: 9.0 days comes from using 9,000 km and not dividing by speed and then by 24.
optionRationale.2: 12.5 days does not follow from the data.
optionRationale.3: 24.5 days does not follow from the data.

questions.objective: Compute time saved by a shorter sea route

questions.stem:
Consider the statements on the WTO.
A. It replaced GATT in 1995.
B. It settles trade disputes among members.
C. It fixes the exchange rate of the currencies of members.
D. Its headquarters are in Geneva.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The WTO replaced GATT in 1995, it settles disputes, and it is headquartered in Geneva, so A, B and D are correct. Exchange rates are not fixed by the WTO, so C is false.

optionRationale.1: C is false, so this pair is wrong.
optionRationale.2: C is false, and A is also correct, so this set is wrong.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so not all four are correct.

questions.stem: Country X has surplus wheat and little oil. Country Y has surplus oil and little wheat. The most appropriate basis for trade between them is
questions.explanation: Trade arises when countries differ in resources, so each has a surplus of what the other lacks. X exports wheat and Y exports oil, and both gain. Similar resources and identical climates would give little reason to trade.

optionRationale.1: Similar resources would reduce the need for trade.
optionRationale.3: Equal population is not the basis of trade.
optionRationale.4: Identical climates would mean similar products and less need to trade.

questions.objective: Apply the resource-difference basis of trade

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of cyberspace?
options: It is formed by networks of connected computers
It reduces the importance of distance in communication
It is a physical territory with fixed national boundaries
questions.explanation: Cyberspace is a virtual world of electronic networks; it enables e-commerce, e-learning and instant communication across distances. It is not a physical territory, so it has no fixed national boundaries of its own.

optionRationale.1: This is a feature, so it is not the exception.
optionRationale.2: This is a feature, so it is not the exception.
optionRationale.3: This is a feature, so it is not the exception.
